title: US manufacturing poised to meet new inverter demand following FCC ban on foreign power inverters
gist: New FCC rules barring approval and sale of new foreign power inverters hit a US solar market where over 90% of the ~200 GW ac of PV inverters delivered in the past decade were imported and Chinese-headquartered vendors held nearly 50% share in 2024-2025; Wood Mackenzie says announced domestic PV/PCS capacity exceeds 100 GW ac by end-2027, so replacement supply should exist but at a price premium that lifts 2027 US inverter prices. The unresolved variable is scope: the ban's definition of 'power inverters' centers on wireless communications, leaving wired utility-scale central inverters ambiguous pending further FCC guidance.

themes.theme: Import dependence and Chinese share of US inverters

insights.claim: More than 90% of the over 200 GW ac of PV inverters delivered to US commercial, industrial and utility-scale projects over the past ten years were imported, making the US solar market structurally dependent on foreign inverter supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Quantifies the switching burden any import restriction imposes: essentially the entire installed inverter base was sourced abroad, so policy risk touches nearly every US solar project owner.
insights.quote: More than 90% of these products were imported, with more than 70 GW coming from Chinese-headquartered manufacturers, mostly delivered from Southeast Asian factories.
insights.locator: Over the past ten years, more than 200 GW

insights.claim: Chinese-headquartered inverter manufacturers supplied more than 70 GW of US PV inverters over the past decade and grew to nearly 50% of US inverter market share in 2024 and 2025, meaning Chinese vendor penetration was still rising right up to the FCC ban.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The share being displaced is roughly half the market and was still gaining, so the addressable revenue pool shifting to non-Chinese suppliers is larger than a static reading of history suggests.
insights.quote: Chinese vendor dominance has grown in recent years, comprising nearly 50% of US inverter market share in 2024 and 2025.

insights.claim: Chinese-headquartered inverter vendors have largely served the US from Southeast Asian factories rather than mainland China, so restrictions keyed to manufacturer headquarters rather than country of shipment are what actually bind.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Tariff- or origin-based workarounds through third countries do not neutralize a headquarters- or security-based rule; watch how the FCC defines the restricted party.
insights.quote: mostly delivered from Southeast Asian factories
insights.locator: More than 90% of these products were imported

themes.theme: Ambiguous scope of the FCC ban

insights.claim: The FCC ban's definition of 'power inverters' is focused on wireless communications, leaving open whether it covers utility-scale central inverters that operate over wired connections.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The single biggest swing factor for utility-scale solar procurement; a wired-inverter carve-out would sharply shrink the volume actually forced to reshore.
insights.quote: the ban's current definition of 'power inverters', focused on wireless communications, leaves real questions about how broadly it will apply, particularly for utility-scale central inverters that operate over wired connections
insights.locator: The FCC's intent here is clear

insights.claim: Leading inverter manufacturers are already telling clients they believe their products fall outside the FCC ban's scope, an industry position that has not yet been tested by FCC guidance.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Vendor reassurance is a self-interested read of an unsettled rule; treat supplier guidance as an unhedged assumption until the FCC clarifies.
insights.quote: Leading manufacturers are notifying clients that they believe their products will not fall under the scope of this ban
insights.locator: Future guidance from the FCC will be crucial

insights.claim: Project owners' acute concern is not new purchases but whether already-installed foreign inverters could be blocked from receiving critical firmware updates, which would turn a procurement rule into an installed-base operating risk.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Creates a potential stranded-asset and O&M cost tail across existing US solar portfolios, not just a forward capex issue; a downside for owners of Chinese-inverter fleets.
insights.quote: project owners are concerned that their existing inverters could be blocked from receiving critical firmware updates
insights.locator: Future guidance from the FCC will be crucial

insights.claim: The US government justified restricting foreign inverters on national security grounds citing both cybersecurity and economic concerns, framing grid-edge power electronics as strategic infrastructure rather than a commodity component.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Signals the restriction template can extend to other networked grid hardware (batteries, meters, controls), so screen the wider power-electronics supply chain for the same policy risk.
insights.quote: The US government determined that the US’s reliance on foreign inverters poses a national security risk, citing both cybersecurity and economic concerns.
insights.locator: The FCC's intent here is clear

themes.theme: Domestic capacity build-out as the offset

insights.claim: Manufacturers have announced plans for more than 100 GW ac of US PV/PCS inverter manufacturing capacity by the end of 2027, which Wood Mackenzie forecasts will be deliverable and sufficient to give project owners compliant alternatives.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A named capacity target and date to track: domestic inverter makers have a policy-protected demand pool if these announcements convert into operating lines.
insights.quote: We forecast the domestic PV/PCS inverter manufacturing market will be able to deliver more than 100 GW ac of capacity by the end of 2027.
insights.locator: If this proves to be a major market shift

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's supply-adequacy call is explicitly conditional on announced capacity materializing, so announced-versus-operating capacity slippage is the key execution risk to the no-shortage view.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Track commissioning milestones rather than press-release capacity; a shortfall converts a price-premium story into a project-delay story.
insights.quote: If materialized, project owners should have safe alternatives, albeit at a premium price
insights.locator: With a market heavily reliant on imported power inverters

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie argues the US is better positioned than ever before to absorb a forced shift to domestic inverter demand, an unusually constructive read on a reshoring shock of this speed.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cuts against the default assumption that an abrupt import ban means project cancellations; the base case here is higher cost, not lost volume.
insights.quote: If this proves to be a major market shift, the US is better positioned now to meet new domestic demand than ever.
insights.locator: The price premium for domestic inverters is a real consideration

themes.theme: Inverter price path and the 45X cliff

insights.claim: Average US inverter prices will rise in 2027 as procurement shifts from lower-cost foreign products to domestic alternatives carrying higher parts, labor and manufacturing costs.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A dated cost-inflation input for 2027 US solar project economics; model higher balance-of-system cost and compressed developer margins for that vintage.
insights.quote: raising average inverter prices in the US in 2027 as procurement moves away from lower-cost foreign products toward domestic alternatives that carry higher costs for parts, labor and manufacturing
insights.locator: A supply chain shift will have consequences

insights.claim: Inverter prices are expected to moderate after the initial 2027 spike as domestic manufacturing scales and competition increases, making the cost shock transitory rather than a permanent step-change.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Argues against extrapolating 2027 inverter pricing into long-dated LCOE models; the premium is a timing problem for near-term project vintages.
insights.locator: Longer term, Wood Mackenzie expects prices to moderate

insights.claim: The phase-out of 45X manufacturing production tax credits from 2030 onwards will add renewed upward pressure on US inverter prices, hitting residential and commercial inverter segments hardest.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Domestic inverter economics have a policy expiry embedded at 2030; the reshoring margin story is subsidised and mean-reverts unless credits are extended.
insights.quote: the phase-out of 45X manufacturing production tax credits from 2030 onwards will add renewed upward pressure, particularly for residential and commercial inverter segments
insights.locator: Longer term, Wood Mackenzie expects prices to moderate

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie frames the domestic inverter price premium as the purchase price of supply chain certainty against any future import-restricting policy, not just the current FCC ban.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Reframes reshoring cost as optionality on further policy escalation, which supports willingness to pay for domestic content beyond the letter of the current rule.
insights.quote: The price premium for domestic inverters is a real consideration for project owners, but it provides supply chain certainty from not only this FCC ban, but from any future policy that could further restrict imports
insights.locator: The price premium for domestic inverters is a real consideration
